rows.evidence: Q1: section 'Farmers' rationale' - repeated in-depth interviews with 12 drip-adopting farmers in Bassi Tehsil, Jaipur District, in 2015 and 2016, plus analysis of GOI/GOR policy. Q2: same section - all 12 farmers reported no reduction in groundwater pumping time or schedules; farmers state they use about the same amount of water or maybe more; farmers with solar wells run both solar and bore-wells; Discussion states findings demonstrate rebound effect with increased rather than decreased groundwater use. Q4: same section - intermediate pathway (intensification and expansion) quantified: irrigated share of cultivable area rose from ~40% to 67% on average after adoption, shift to water-intensive chilies, greenhouses adding a third cropping season. Q6: unit of observation is the farm/household (12 farms, 1.38-6.33 ha) across one administrative block, not a single plot. Q7: Abstract, Introduction and Conclusions - author states from the findings that drip will not lead to water savings in the absence of groundwater-use rules/institutional arrangements; the regulatory vacuum and incentives to intensify are stated as the conditions producing the harmful effect.
rows.notes: Evidence is qualitative farmer self-report (interviews), not measured pumping volumes or groundwater levels. Q3: single method (interviews); policy-document analysis does not bear on the effect. Q5: one tehsil, one region. Q6 is borderline (farm scale only, 12 farms); Q8: study mentions that reliable area data are unavailable and that 12 farmers were nearly the whole adopter population, but does not frame these as limitations of its result. Q9: no dispersion for the water-use result; only ranges for landholding size and subsidy rates.

rows.evidence: Q1: section 'Farmers' rationale' - own interviews with 12 drip adopters in Bassi Tehsil, 2015-2016. Q2: same section - farmers adopted drip to intensify and expand production, report no reduction in pumping, are aware water demand is growing with negative impacts on groundwater recharge; one farmer expects water to be depleted beyond the solar pump in three years; Rajasthan described as having no formal regulation limiting pumping (section 'Groundwater in Rajasthan'). Q4: same section - mechanism quantified: irrigated area share rose from ~40% to 67%, shift to water-intensive chilies and greenhouse off-season crops. Q6: farm/household-level results across 12 farms in one administrative block. Q7: Abstract and Conclusions - author states that without groundwater-use rules drip adoption will not save water and leads to further mining; absence of regulation stated as the condition for the harmful outcome.
rows.notes: Claim is about over-extraction worsening recharge problems; the study's own evidence is farmer self-report of unchanged or increased pumping and expanded irrigated area, not measured groundwater levels or recharge. Single method, single site, no stated limitations of own result, no dispersion measure.

rows.evidence: Q1: section 'Farmers' rationale' - repeated interviews with 12 drip-adopting farmers in Bassi Tehsil, 2015 and 2016. Q2: Discussion - findings presented demonstrate the operation of the Jevons paradox/rebound effect, where drip adoption led to increased rather than decreased groundwater use; farmers reported no reduction in pumping and the same or more water use. Q4: 'Farmers' rationale' section - reallocation of savings quantified via irrigated area rising from ~40% to 67% of cultivable area, denser row spacing/fertigation, greenhouses adding a cropping season, new water-intensive chili production. Q6: results at farm/household scale across 12 farms in one block. Q7: Introduction and Conclusions - author states drip will not conserve water on its own or in the absence of new institutional arrangements (groundwater usage rules); regulatory vacuum stated as condition for the rebound.
rows.notes: The passage says the paradox has been observed in various contexts; this study documents it in only one context (one tehsil in Rajasthan) and otherwise cites other work (Ward & Pulido-Velazquez; Dumont et al.), which does not count. Evidence is self-reported, no measurement, no triangulation, no stated limitations, no dispersion.

notes: Full text appears complete. Qualitative political-ecology case study: 12 farmer interviews (snowball sample, near-total adopter population in Bassi Tehsil) plus policy review. Water-use results are farmer self-reports rather than measured abstraction or groundwater levels; all three claim rows draw on the same evidence base and receive the same profile.
